teaser.text: Lloyds Banking Group is a mainly British financial-services business: it takes in deposits, lends money, and sells protection, savings and investment services. A pound enters as interest, a fee or an insurance premium, and leaves as funding cost, claim, loss or operating expense before the remainder becomes profit.

stock.opening: Lloyds's probability-weighted price is 113,254.26 GBp in October 2029, with 30% bear, 50% base and 20% bull. It hinges on redress staying within provision, hedge reinvestment sustaining income, and fee growth and AI savings becoming recurring.

blocks.heading: Where could Lloyds's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The probability-weighted price is 92,512.96 GBp in October 2027, 101,622.19 GBp in October 2028 and 113,254.26 GBp in October 2029. Including dividends, those outcomes represent returns of 90,960%, 99,929% and 111,382% from today’s 101.60. The October 2029 range runs from 48,854.12 GBp in the bear case to 176,109.29 GBp in the bull case. The probabilities are 30% bear, 50% base and 20% bull.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Lloyds?

paragraphs.text: Book value is the first driver. The base case rises from £44,661m in October 2027 to £47,761m and then £51,161m. It assumes retained earnings exceed dividends and buybacks, with earnings of £7.4bn and £7.8bn in the following periods. The starting point is credible because the next-12-month EPS estimate implies roughly £7.2bn of earnings at about 59bn shares. The bear case gives £40,121m, £40,221m and £40,521m because extra redress, credit losses and distributions absorb most earnings. The bull case gives £45,561m, £48,861m and £52,461m because fee income, hedge income and efficiency gains support stronger profits. The range reflects Lloyds’ uneven equity history and the £1.95bn motor-finance provision.

The bull case requires redress to remain within provision, hedge reinvestment to sustain income, and AI savings, cross-selling and fee growth to become recurring. Larger buybacks and a 1.80x book multiple then lift the price from 123,160.03 GBp to 176,109.29 GBp. Its 20% probability reflects the number of conditions that must align; a 17.1% half-year RoTE is encouraging but does not prove full-cycle delivery.

dividend.meta_description: Lloyds dividend payments, cash coverage, risks and yield in one clear view.
dividend.opening: Lloyds pays a 1.58p interim dividend; its base-case annual dividends rise from 3.85p to 4.10p and 4.35p. Lloyds' dividend is supported when retained earnings exceed dividends and buybacks, but redress and credit costs can constrain distributions.
dividend.closing: The full Lloyds memo also explains its business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does Lloyds pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends rise in the base case from 3.85p to 4.10p and 4.35p. That follows five years of increases and management’s progressive, sustainable policy, while remaining conditional on capital needs. The bear case gives 3.00p, 2.70p and 2.80p as redress and credit costs constrain distributions. The bull case gives 4.20p, 4.60p and 5.00p because stronger earnings and capital generation fund faster increases. The latest 1.58p interim dividend supports the base run rate, but the £322m latest-quarter impairment charge shows why the bear remains credible.

paragraphs.text: The forecast moves toward the bear case if redress exceeds £1.95bn during October 2027–October 2028, because charges reduce profit, capital generation and buybacks. Deposit repricing and mortgage competition would weaken net interest income through 2027–2029, while a UK downturn from 2028 would raise impairments and compress the multiple.

blocks.heading: What is Lloyds' dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: The 3.6% dividend yield is backward-looking. Lloyds announced a 1.58p interim dividend, a further £1 billion buyback and continued commitment to a progressive dividend policy. The question is whether future earnings and capital can support those distributions while motor-finance risk remains unresolved.

blocks.heading: What has Lloyds guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Management has raised its strategic-initiative revenue promise to £2 billion by the end of 2026 and targets return on tangible equity above 16%. Return on tangible equity measures profit against shareholders’ tangible capital, so the two promises belong together: extra revenue matters only if enough survives as profit.

The first half supports the plan. Return on tangible equity reached 17.1%, other income grew 11% and operating costs stayed broadly flat. The full-year tests remain underlying net interest income above £14.9 billion, operating costs below £9.9 billion and a cost:income ratio below 50%. That ratio shows how much income operating costs consume.

blocks.heading: Did Lloyds keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Delay matters because bad decisions can look successful at first. Deferred awards and provisions to reduce or recover them allow later losses or customer harm to affect pay. Lloyds said it met around 80% of its strategic outcome targets for 2024. For 2025, the remuneration committee reduced the financial score from 81.9% to 74.0% after considering the motor-finance provision, even though that provision had been excluded from the original bonus measures.

blocks.heading: How has Lloyds' revenue and profit changed over the last eight quarters?

paragraphs.text: Revenue reached £5,442 million, up 16.0% year on year. Net interest income reached £3,622 million, and its steady quarterly progression since September 2024 is stronger evidence than one unusually good period.

After-tax profit was £1,568 million, while diluted EPS was 2.40p. The bad-loan charge rose to £322 million from £132 million, although the comparison starts from an unusually favourable provision period.
